rows.en: Chapter Twenty-Five
The destruction of the Temple.

Amid political and religious disputes and quarrels the last decades of the days of the Temple passed, and they hastened its destruction and the destruction of the land of Judah and its people. Indeed, the marks of their downfall were already visible before this. Throughout the days of Herod, Judah was still a respected kingdom in the eyes of the peoples around it, and so it was in its own eyes, even though the authority of Rome was over it; but from the day of Herod's death his dominion fell to pieces, and those who came after him were nothing but instruments of violence in the hands of the Romans. The rod of Rome rested on the lot of Israel, and they groaned under the oppression of its procurators, and the would-be rulers of the house of Herod could not save them. The violence of their oppressors grew from day to day, and they made the yoke of taxes so heavy on them that they could not bear it. The procurators, greedy for their wealth, robbed the people by laying hands on all their property and possessions. They interfered in their religious and legal affairs and curtailed the power of the Sanhedrin. After the death of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder (Pe'ah 2:6), and perhaps already at the end of his life, they [the Sanhedrin] were forced to leave their seat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone and sat in the Ḥanut (Sanhedrin 41a), and this continued all the days of Rabban Simeon his son (Keritot 5a). They [the Romans] appointed and also removed high priests as their greed demanded, and it is self-evident that they set their eye and heart not on fitness but on gain. Therefore most of the high priests who were appointed at that time were men of violence, as were those who appointed them (Pesaḥim 57a). This evil state was the reason why the strength to endure failed; the zeal of the people was roused, and a revolt blazed up that has no equal in the annals of the ancient peoples. But because the revolt was not led with one heart and one mind, and quarrels and strife broke out among them anew every morning, it did not succeed. In the intoxication of their zeal they were confused and did not know what a time as dangerous as theirs demanded of them. This confusion was their undoing and the undoing of their hope; myriads upon thousands, innocent and not innocent, fell slain at its feet. It caused the Romans to defeat them with a complete victory: they conquered all the fortified cities in Judah and made their land a desolation, and they went on in their victory from strength to strength until the royal city too was conquered before them, and Zion and Jerusalem became "a ruinous heap" [Isaiah 17:1], the Temple of the Lord was burned with fire, and the Jews were scattered to the four winds of heaven.

Like a flaming fire the revolt seized all hearts together: officers and the poor of the people, sages and common men, all were among the conspirators. But a small remnant of the sages, most of them of the House of Hillel, the gentle and the humble, did not have their eyes shut from seeing nor their hearts from understanding [cf. Isaiah 44:18] that they would have no standing before the Romans. They understood well and knew the whole strength of their enemies, who were all trained in war and skilled in battle; and beside them, what did the Jews count for, a people despised and plundered, a people divided by disputes, whose good forces had been weakened by groundless hatred (Yoma 9a)? With grief of soul they also looked on the religious conflicts of that time: on the division of the Jews within, who had turned from their fathers' faith in the One God of the world and had broken the covenant of the flesh, the Sabbath and all the practical commandments of the Torah (Lamentations Rabbah, on "Eikhah yashvah"); the disputes of the Houses, too, were a grief of spirit to them, for they had changed their character from what they had been formerly: no longer, as at first, were they conducted calmly and in love of truth and peace; rather, they overstepped the bounds of uprightness, and the House of Shammai turned peace into wormwood, and strife and contention raised their head. Seeing these things, the wise saw that their downfall was complete and decreed, and they bowed their head before the terrible burden that the Lord had laid on Israel. Yet they did not despair altogether, for the Jews have always been a people schooled in hope. Even if their breach was "great like the sea" [Lamentations 2:13], greater still was their trust in the God of their fathers that He would not forsake them forever. Therefore this time too the discerning among the people, the gentle and the deliberate, did not give up hope for their future, but hoped that the remnant of survivors that was left was the remnant "whom the Lord calls" [Joel 3:5] to give endurance to the weary nation and to the Torah; "not by might, nor by power, but by" spirit [Zechariah 4:6] will Israel be saved. The signs that they had seen and foretold came with terrible speed, and with the fall of Zion and Jerusalem the last spark of their political freedom was extinguished; but with "help from the sanctuary" [Psalms 20:3] the Torah and the religion were saved out of the upheaval.

Yet even if it is true that the surviving sages saved the Torah for the generations to come, nevertheless it cannot be denied that the last events had a great effect on the Oral Torah. For a great number of the sages perished by the sword, by famine, in captivity and in plunder, and they were the bearers of the Oral Torah; and how could it be that when the helper stumbles the one helped would not fall too [cf. Isaiah 31:3], and that the loss of many of its bearers would not harm the Oral Torah? And indeed so it was. Already in the first generation after the destruction they complained of the loss of the wisdom of the sages because of the events and the hardships (Sotah 49a), and the deliberate sages, whose eyes were not too dim to see the end of a matter from its beginning, understood from the start that the danger was near that the Torah would be forgotten. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, one of the disciples of Hillel, versed in Torah and in wisdom (Yerushalmi Nedarim 5:7; Sukkah 28a) and laden with commandments (Yerushalmi Berakhot 2:3), who loved peace with every man (Berakhot 17), was counted among the Sanhedrin in the days of the Temple (Sanhedrin 40b), spread Torah among the many in the streets of the city (Pesaḥim 26a) and in his great house of study (Lamentations Rabbah, Proem), was one of the counsellors of peace with the Romans (Gittin 56a), and preached in praise of peace between a man and his fellow, between city and city, between nation and nation, between government and government, and between family and family (Mekhilta Yitro ch. 11): this great man{v1_12_24:1} recognized that in the events of his time a great danger lay for the survival of the Oral Torah, and with a worried heart he lamented: "A later generation is destined to declare pure the impure thing whose impurity has no scriptural basis in the Torah" (Sotah 27b). There is no doubt that when he lamented thus he had before his eyes all the dangers lying in wait for the teaching of the Pharisees, from enemies new and old: the Sadducees, and the Jews who had separated from among their brethren and become a sect of their own; for both of these had written on their banner eternal enmity to the Oral Torah. His worry about the Sadducees was justified, because at the end of the days of the Temple they once more raised their head and held the high priesthood (Tosefta Parah ch. 2), and harassed the Pharisees with debates to dispute their teaching (Bava Batra 115a; Menaḥot 65b; Yadayim 4:6). Likewise his worry about the other Jews who differed in their opinion was justified, for in his days sectarianism had a power of attraction among the Jews. And no small stumbling block in his eyes were the disputes among the Pharisees themselves, which grew stronger in the days of the revolt, because the disciples of the House of Shammai supported the violent men more than the House of Hillel did, and therefore they in turn were strengthened in their dispute by the violent men. All these worries about the forgetting of the Oral Torah grew stronger still in the heart of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai when he considered the nature of this Torah, which is carried only by memory and whose survival depends on the survival of those who carry it. How then should he not worry that it would diminish and be forgotten little by little, at a time when its bearers and expounders were growing fewer and fewer and stumbling "by the sword and by flame, by captivity" [Daniel 11:33] and by famine, and when he saw moreover that most of this Torah was hanging in the air and had no scripture in the Torah to rely on? All this was a task for Rabban Yoḥanan with which to afflict his spirit; and therefore he exerted all his strength to stand up against all these harms and to overcome them as far as his hand could. When he saw at the end of the days of the siege that the fall of Jerusalem was near, he devised a stratagem to escape from the turmoil. His wish succeeded with the help of his disciples and friends: he escaped out through the city gate, reached the enemy lines without harm, and stood before Vespasian, the commander of the Roman armies at that time. This commander knew the state of affairs within besieged Jerusalem, and knew who belonged to the counsellors of peace and who to those for war, and he also knew that Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai was not among the conspirators but always counselled peace; therefore he was honoured in the eyes of Vespasian, who received him with grace and kindness and promised to do whatever he would ask of him. Now there is no doubt that he could have obtained at that time freedoms⚠1 and many privileges, but his eye and heart were not set on all the political benefits and temporal matters; only his worry about the forgetting of the Torah put words in his mouth and moved his request. Therefore he asked only for the thing most necessary for the survival of the religion: that he grant him permission to maintain the study of the Torah, to gather his disciples to Yavneh and to establish a house of study there (Gittin 56a), to set up a place of prayer, and that they not be hindered from walking in the ways of the Torah and in its commandments (Avot de-Rabbi Natan ch. 4).

rows.en: And just as the fear that the Oral Torah would be forgotten was the cause that moved Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's request before Vespasian and the impulse for his efforts and his work from then on, so this fear also filled the heart of the remaining sages of his generation and roused their spirit to seek the way by which to secure the survival of the Oral Torah, that it not be forgotten and not be defeated by its opponents. This way the surviving sages found out of the upheaval immediately after the destruction. Their first work was to collect the halakhot that were in their memory, to save them from oblivion: not only halakhot on matters in force in every place and at every time, but also halakhot that no longer had any standing after the destruction; and for some sages the main occupation was with such halakhot and their arrangement. In the halakhot that remained in force they searched and inquired to know their reasons and their rationale and to understand their consequences; but to break the force of the opposition to the Oral Torah they endeavoured to show a source in the written Torah for the principles of all the halakhot. To achieve this, the ways of midrash were widened much more than they had been before. This widening was prepared and founded by the surviving sages, especially in the house of study of R. Neḥunya ben ha-Kanah and Naḥum of Gimzo, and it reached its completion through their disciples R. Akiva and R. Ishmael. By their method they succeeded in expounding heaps upon heaps of halakhot on every tittle of the Torah, and they showed that the whole mass of halakhot followed from the Torah of Moses. Therefore the Oral Torah was now no longer the teaching of the elders, nor, as its opponents called it, "a commandment of men learned by rote" [Isaiah 29:13]. Rather, since its foundation lay in the Torah, it had the standing of the statutes and ordinances written in the Torah; and since they believed that their interpretation was the meaning truly intended in the words of Scripture, they could rightly refute the claim of the opponents of the Oral Torah by telling them that their teaching was not something new that men had devised out of their own heart, but was the original intent of the words of Scripture. Now we understand the sight we meet in the first generation after the destruction, when the midrash of the Torah suddenly widens without limit, and we know that it not only reached a new stage but also reached the stage of its completion. This is not the place for me to speak of every detail of the general aspects to which we have alluded briefly; but when we reach the generation after the destruction the matters will be clarified and explained with compelling proofs. We have touched on them here only with the tip of the staff of our inquiry, so that we may recognize the great effect that the events at the end of the days of the Temple and its destruction had on the Oral Torah, and see with our own eyes that together with the nation's temporal happiness the spiritual heritage that they had inherited from their fathers was not lost; on the contrary, now all the good forces united to establish this heritage, to strengthen its pegs, to raise its horn and to consecrate it as holy.

Then the Oral Torah was the aim of their thoughts; to it they devoted all their strength, their lives and their substance. It was their hope and it was their glory. The desire to serve it and to guard it from the blows of time and from the obstacles set by its opponents was strong and firm within them, beyond anything like it in the times before them and after them. The memory of this work of theirs and of the goal they attained by it was holy to all the generations that came after; it was "a cup of consolation" [Jeremiah 16:7] in their hand in all the terrible hardships that befell them in the lands of their dispersion. But this memory also gives us the measure for our own deeds. Like them, we too shall not "hide our hand in the dish" [Proverbs 19:24] if the events and the course of the times require our labour on the soil of this Torah bequeathed to us by our fathers; according to this course, and according to the changes that it has drawn after it, we shall direct our steps on this holy ground. For then, from beneath the heaps of dust that have piled up on it over many days, the spirit of the Jewish religion will renew its youth and "mount up with wings as eagles" [Isaiah 40:31], as in those days too it rose to new life out of the ruins of Jerusalem.

footnotes.en: I have seen fit to call attention here to a valuable article in Graetz's monthly journal of the year 1870, May issue, p. 238, by Rabbi David Oppenheim⚠1, which contains a critique of Renan's book on the history of the Apostles, and especially of what he copied there from the words of Rabbi Jacob Emden in his glosses to *Seder Olam*, which was published in Hamburg in the year 5517 [1757].

footnotes.en: The chief work of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai came after the destruction, and at the beginning of the second part of this work of ours we shall give a place to his memory. Here we mention only what must be known now in relation to the end of the days of the Temple and its destruction.
